meta.title: AQA GCSE Geography (8035) question bank with self-check rubrics
meta.verification_note: Specification points follow the AQA 8035 subject content (key ideas). Marking conventions were sampled from five AQA mark schemes (8035/1 2022 & 2023, 8035/2 2022 & 2023, 8035/3 2023). Individual questions and accepted-answer lists have not been verified against every past paper.
meta.options_note: All optional content is included; filter on the question 'option' field (hot deserts / cold environments; two of coasts / rivers / glacial; one of food / water / energy).

self_check_matching_spec.purpose: Pre-tick rubric criteria from a student's typed answer. It is a suggestion: the student confirms each tick, and a teacher (independent_met) can overrule it. It should be generous to alternative phrasing but must not credit negated, do-not-accept or off-topic answers.
reference_implementation: pengine.py (normalisation, token matching, keyword rules, negation, proximity)
pipeline: 1. Normalise the answer with norm_text (below) into a token list. Rule phrases are normalised the same way, so both sides use the same canonical words.
2. For each criterion, run its one rule: keyword_rules, idea_score_rule or numeric_rule.
3. A criterion is suggested as met if its rule passes. The suggested mark is the sum of met criteria marks.

4. Levels questions (marking_style = 'levels'): each criterion is one level-mark 'slot' (ideas, developed ideas, both sides, specific detail, judgement). Sum the ticks and map to levels[] (min_marks..max_marks). level_caps are shown to the student as self-check prompts; they are not auto-applied.

steps: CONTRACTIONS (regex, in order): can't -> cannot, n't -> not, ...
PHRASE_CANON (regex, in order): multi-word everyday phrases -> canonical words, eg 'fall down' -> collapse, 'not many' -> few, 'panels on the roof' -> solar panels
superscripts; unicode NFKC; strip accents; % -> ' percent '; ° -> ' degrees '; → and -> -> ' so '; & and + -> ' and '
remove thousands separators (10,000 -> 10000); digit/digit -> two numbers; digit:digit -> two numbers (ratios kept)
punctuation , ; : ! ? and sentence full stops -> the token 'brk' (a clause boundary used by negation and development scoring)
split on whitespace; NUMW, UK spelling (UKSP), then TOKEN_CANON (vernacular single words -> canonical word, eg 'quake' -> earthquake, 'flimsy' -> weak, 'kids' -> children)
PHRASE_CANON: \b(?:cannot|unable to|not able to) (?:afford|pay for|pay)\b|\b(?:too|very) expensive for\b
\bnot as (?:many|much)\b|\bnot (?:many|much)\b|\bhardly any\b|\bnot a lot of\b|\bvery few\b|\bvery little\b|\bnot enough\b|\binsufficient\b|\binadequate\b
\bmiles from anywhere\b|\bmiddle of nowhere\b|\bfar from (?:anywhere|everything|towns|cities)\b|\bout of the way\b
\b(?:come|comes|coming|go|goes|active|only) out (?:at|during the) night\b|\bactive at night\b|\bat night time\b

\b(?:wear|wears|wearing|wore|worn) (?:it |them |the rock |the rocks |the cliff |the land |the stones? )?(?:away|down|back)\b|\beat(?:s|ing)? (?:away|into)\b|\bate (?:away|into)\b|\bchip(?:s|ped|ping)? away\b|\bgnaw(?:s|ed|ing)? away\b
\b(?:miles|far|a long way) (?:away )?from where (?:it|they) (?:came from|started|formed|was from)\b|\bfrom somewhere else\b|\bfrom far away\b
\bmore than (?:it|they|the waves?) takes? away\b|\btake away less\b
\b(?:costs?|costing|cost) (?:a fortune|loads|a lot|tons|a bomb|so much|too much|lots)\b|\b(?:very|really|super) expensive\b

token_match.description: Answer token s matches rule token a if any of these hold (checked in order):
rules: both numeric and equal as numbers; if only one is numeric -> no match
the pair is in CONFUSABLE -> NO match (stops eg increase/decrease, erosion/corrosion, warming/warning being treated as typos)
len(a) >= 3 and s = a + one of SUFFIXES (eg erode -> eroded; protect -> protection)
len >= 3 for both and stem(s) == stem(a) (and the stem is not just 2 letters)
typo: len(a) >= 5, |len(s)-len(a)| <= 2, same first letter, Damerau-Levenshtein distance <= 1 (<= 2 if len(a) >= 9)
token_match.stem: if len<4 or numeric: unchanged. -bility -> -ble; drop -al (not -ial/-eal, stem >= 4); then first of ies->y, ied->y, ing, ed, es, s (not -ss), ly (remaining stem >= 3, or >= 2 for ies/ied); drop final e (len >= 4); undouble a final consonant other than l/s (len >= 4)

phrase_syntax.plain phrase: 'poorly built' - consecutive tokens, each by token_match
phrase_syntax.pipe alternatives: 'house|houses|homes' - any one of the options (options may be multi-word)
phrase_syntax.proximity: 'house|homes ~ poorly built|weak' - every part must be found, each within WINDOW tokens of the first part's match, in ANY order
phrase_syntax.=X: the whole normalised answer must equal X (used for MCQ letters, so 'C' scores but 'C or D' does not)
phrase_syntax.@concept: expanded at BUILD time from the lexicon; the rules in the JSON are already expanded, so the app never needs the lexicon to mark

negation.applies_when: the rule (or its parent for or-branches) has negation_sensitive = true
negation.rule: a matched phrase does NOT count if (a) one of not/never/cannot/t follows it within the next 4 tokens with only AUX words between ('houses are not weak'), or (b) a NEGATORS word occurs up to 5 tokens before it, with no BREAKS word between ('no houses were weak'). A phrase that itself starts with a negator ('not earthquake proof', 'no warning') is never treated as negated. For proximity phrases, the combination is accepted if any chosen part starts with a negator, or no chosen part is negated; candidates are tried nearest-first, preferring negator-led options and non-negated hits.
negation.measured: about 94% of seed phrases are correctly rejected when negated in validation templates (see validation_report.json negated_seed_tests)

shape.all_of: [[alt, alt, ...], [alt, ...]] - every group needs at least one matching alternative
shape.none_of: [alt, ...] - if any matches, the rule fails
shape.or: [rule, ...] - alternative full rules; branches inherit the parent's none_of and negation_sensitive

keyword_rules.met: core(all_of, none_of) passes, or any or-branch passes

idea_score_rule.purpose: AQA point marking: 1 mark per valid point, and/or 1 mark for each point that is developed (d).

fields.ideas: [{idea_id, label, keyword_rules, development_rules?}] - the creditable points (from the mark scheme's indicative content)
fields.connectives: linking words; developments only count if at least one is present
fields.development_rules: question-level rule for a development (negation_sensitive false)
fields.generic_development: {splitters, consequence_words}: a clause starting after a splitter (excluding weak splitters) that contains a consequence word counts as a development
fields.count_all_ideas: false = only one idea can count ('Outline one ...')
fields.min_score: the criterion is met when score >= min_score. A 3-mark question has three criteria with min_score 1, 2, 3, so the suggested mark is the score capped at the max

algorithm: For each idea, find all token spans where its keyword_rules match (rule_spans_all).
One phrase can support only one idea: ideas with fewer candidate spans choose first, each taking a span that does not overlap words already used.
ideas_score = number of ideas hit (or min(1, n) if count_all_ideas is false).

dev_score (only if a connective is present): ideas whose own development_rules match, or the question development_rules match; then dev_score = max(dev_score, min(generic_developments, ideas_hit)). Capped at 1 if count_all_ideas is false.
score = ideas, developments or ideas + developments according to score_mode.
idea_score_rule.mark_scheme_link: Matches AQA conventions: '1 mark per valid point, extra mark for development'; 'two basic statements gain 2'; 'Outline one' = point + development.

numeric_rule.fields: expected_value, accepted_units, absolute_tolerance, relative_tolerance, unit_required, accept_range
numeric_rule.met: a number in the answer is within tolerance or inside accept_range (inclusive); units are accepted but optional unless unit_required. Unevaluated expressions (eg '54/2') are not credited.

levels_questions.criteria: each is an idea_score_rule slot worth 1 level-mark: relevant ideas (i), developed ideas (d), both sides / both areas (b), specific case-study detail (s), justified judgement (j).
levels_questions.judgement_rule: a judgement word (agree, disagree, more important, I think, overall, to a large extent, ...) plus a reason connective (because/as/since/so).
levels_questions.honesty: Levels marking is holistic in AQA. The ticks are a structured self-check guide; level_caps and SPaG (spag_marks) are prompts, not auto-applied.

self_check_matching_spec.conformance_tests: Every criterion carries examples[] (must be met) and reject_examples[] (must not be met). questions[].self_check.marking_notes lists do-not-accept answers from the mark schemes, which must score 0. A port is conformant when it reproduces the reference results on all of them.

soil_erosion: soil ~ erode|erosion|eroded|washed away|wash away|blown away|blow away|lost|loss|removed

specification_points.title: Natural hazards: definition, types and factors affecting hazard risk

misconceptions.misconception: Hazards are only the physical event.
misconceptions.feedback: A hazard is a natural event that threatens people or property; risk depends on vulnerability too.

misconceptions.misconception: Hazard risk depends only on how strong the event is.
misconceptions.feedback: Risk also depends on population density, wealth, preparation and urbanisation.

specification_points.title: Plate tectonics theory, distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes, plate margins

misconceptions.misconception: Plates float on molten lava.
misconceptions.feedback: Plates move on the semi-molten mantle, driven by convection currents / slab pull.

misconceptions.misconception: Volcanoes occur at conservative margins.
misconceptions.feedback: Conservative margins produce earthquakes but not volcanoes - no magma is created.

specification_points.title: Primary and secondary effects and immediate and long-term responses to a tectonic hazard in contrasting areas

misconceptions.misconception: Secondary effects happen at the same time as the earthquake.
misconceptions.feedback: Primary effects are caused directly by the shaking; secondary effects follow from them (fires, disease, landslides).

misconceptions.misconception: Richer countries always have more deaths because more is built.
misconceptions.feedback: HICs usually have fewer deaths but higher economic costs.

specification_points.title: Why people live in areas at risk; monitoring, prediction, protection and planning

misconceptions.misconception: Earthquakes can be predicted accurately.
misconceptions.feedback: Earthquakes cannot be predicted exactly; monitoring helps for volcanoes.

misconceptions.misconception: People who live near volcanoes do not know the risk.
misconceptions.feedback: Many stay because of fertile soils, jobs, tourism, geothermal energy or attachment to home.

specification_points.title: Global atmospheric circulation: pressure belts and surface winds

misconceptions.misconception: Air rises at 30° north and south.
misconceptions.feedback: Air sinks at about 30° (high pressure); it rises at the equator and 60° (low pressure).

misconceptions.misconception: Winds blow from low to high pressure.
misconceptions.feedback: Surface winds blow from high to low pressure.

specification_points.title: Tropical storms: distribution, causes, formation, structure and climate change

misconceptions.misconception: Tropical storms form over land.
misconceptions.feedback: They form over warm oceans (about 27°C) and weaken over land.

misconceptions.misconception: The eye is the most violent part.
misconceptions.feedback: The eye is calm with sinking air; the eyewall has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.

specification_points.title: Tropical storms: effects, responses, and reducing the effects

misconceptions.misconception: Most deaths are caused by wind.
misconceptions.feedback: Storm surges and flooding usually cause most deaths.

misconceptions.misconception: Nothing can be done to reduce the effects.
misconceptions.feedback: Monitoring, prediction, protection and planning all reduce effects.

specification_points.title: UK weather hazards, an extreme weather event and evidence that UK weather is becoming more extreme

misconceptions.misconception: The UK has no weather hazards.
misconceptions.feedback: The UK has floods, storms, droughts, heatwaves, snow and cold spells.

misconceptions.misconception: One extreme event proves climate change.
misconceptions.feedback: Evidence needs trends over time, eg more record temperatures and more frequent heavy rain.

specification_points.title: Climate change: evidence, natural and human causes, effects

misconceptions.misconception: The greenhouse effect is caused by the hole in the ozone layer.
misconceptions.feedback: It is caused by gases such as CO2 and methane trapping heat.

misconceptions.misconception: Climate has never changed before humans.
misconceptions.feedback: Natural causes (orbital changes, volcanic activity, solar output) have changed climate throughout the Quaternary.

specification_points.title: Managing climate change: mitigation and adaptation

misconceptions.misconception: Mitigation and adaptation mean the same thing.
misconceptions.feedback: Mitigation reduces the causes; adaptation responds to the effects.

misconceptions.misconception: Planting trees is adaptation.
misconceptions.feedback: Planting trees absorbs CO2 so it is mitigation.

specification_points.title: Ecosystems: components, food chains and webs, nutrient cycling, balance and change

misconceptions.misconception: Decomposers are consumers at the top of the food chain.
misconceptions.feedback: Decomposers break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil.

misconceptions.misconception: Changing one component only affects that species.
misconceptions.feedback: Ecosystems are interdependent so a change spreads through the food web.

specification_points.title: Distribution and characteristics of large-scale global ecosystems

misconceptions.misconception: Rainforests are found in all hot countries.
misconceptions.feedback: Rainforests lie near the Equator, between the tropics, where it is hot and wet all year.

misconceptions.misconception: Deserts are always hot.
misconceptions.feedback: Hot deserts lie near 30° N and S; there are also cold deserts.

specification_points.title: Tropical rainforests: characteristics, interdependence, adaptations and biodiversity

misconceptions.misconception: Rainforest soils are very fertile.
misconceptions.feedback: Soils are thin and nutrient-poor; most nutrients are in the biomass.

misconceptions.misconception: Rainforests have four distinct seasons.
misconceptions.feedback: It is hot and wet all year with little seasonal change.

specification_points.title: Deforestation: changing rates, causes and impacts

misconceptions.misconception: Deforestation is only caused by logging.
misconceptions.feedback: Farming (cattle, soya, palm oil), mining, roads, energy and settlement also cause it.

misconceptions.misconception: Deforestation has no economic benefits.
misconceptions.feedback: It brings income, jobs and development, but has environmental costs.

specification_points.title: Value of rainforests and strategies to manage them sustainably

misconceptions.misconception: Sustainable management means no use of the forest.
misconceptions.feedback: It means using the forest without damaging it for future generations.

misconceptions.misconception: Ecotourism has no impact at all.
misconceptions.feedback: It is small scale and low impact, and brings income that encourages conservation.

specification_points.title: Hot deserts: characteristics, interdependence, adaptations and biodiversity

misconceptions.misconception: Hot deserts are hot at night.
misconceptions.feedback: Clear skies mean nights can be very cold; the daily temperature range is large.

misconceptions.misconception: Nothing lives in deserts.
misconceptions.feedback: Plants and animals are adapted, eg cacti store water and camels conserve water.

specification_points.title: Hot deserts: opportunities and challenges for development

misconceptions.misconception: Deserts offer no economic opportunities.
misconceptions.feedback: Mineral extraction, solar energy, farming with irrigation and tourism are opportunities.

misconceptions.misconception: Water is no problem if you drill wells.
misconceptions.feedback: Groundwater is limited and can be over-abstracted.

specification_points.title: Desertification: causes and strategies to reduce the risk

misconceptions.misconception: Desertification means deserts moving.
misconceptions.feedback: It is land degradation in dry areas so land becomes more desert-like.

misconceptions.misconception: Desertification is only caused by climate.
misconceptions.feedback: Overgrazing, over-cultivation, fuel wood removal and population growth also cause it.

specification_points.title: Cold environments: characteristics, interdependence, adaptations and biodiversity

misconceptions.misconception: Polar and tundra are the same.
misconceptions.feedback: Tundra has a short summer with some plant growth; polar areas are colder and mostly ice.

misconceptions.misconception: Permafrost thaws completely each summer.
misconceptions.feedback: Only the active layer thaws; the permafrost below stays frozen.

specification_points.title: Cold environments: opportunities and challenges for development

misconceptions.misconception: Cold environments have nothing of value.
misconceptions.feedback: Oil, gas, minerals, fishing and tourism are opportunities.

misconceptions.misconception: Building is easy once you clear snow.
misconceptions.feedback: Buildings can melt permafrost and subside, so they are raised on piles.

specification_points.title: Value of cold environments as wilderness and strategies to protect them

misconceptions.misconception: Wilderness areas have no value.
misconceptions.feedback: They have scientific, ecological and aesthetic value and are fragile.

misconceptions.misconception: Only governments protect cold environments.
misconceptions.feedback: International agreements (eg Antarctic Treaty), technology and conservation groups also help.

specification_points.title: UK physical landscapes: upland and lowland areas and river systems

misconceptions.misconception: The UK uplands are in the south east.
misconceptions.feedback: Uplands are mainly in the north and west (Scotland, Lake District, Pennines, Wales).

misconceptions.misconception: Lowland areas are made of hard rock.
misconceptions.feedback: Lowlands are mostly softer, younger rocks such as clay and chalk.

specification_points.title: Coastal processes: waves, weathering, mass movement, erosion, transportation and deposition

misconceptions.misconception: Constructive waves erode the beach.
misconceptions.feedback: Constructive waves have a strong swash and build up beaches; destructive waves erode.

misconceptions.misconception: Weathering and erosion are the same.
misconceptions.feedback: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion wears it away and removes it.

specification_points.title: Coastal landforms of erosion and deposition

misconceptions.misconception: Headlands are made of soft rock.
misconceptions.feedback: Headlands are made of more resistant rock which erodes more slowly.

misconceptions.misconception: A stack is formed directly from a cave.
misconceptions.feedback: Cave, then arch, then the arch collapses leaving a stack.

specification_points.title: Coastal management: hard and soft engineering, managed retreat, a UK scheme

misconceptions.misconception: Groynes stop longshore drift completely along the whole coast.
misconceptions.feedback: They trap sediment locally and can starve beaches further down the coast.

misconceptions.misconception: Soft engineering means weak defences.
misconceptions.feedback: Soft engineering works with natural processes, eg beach nourishment.

specification_points.title: River long and cross profiles and fluvial processes

misconceptions.misconception: Rivers erode most in the lower course.
misconceptions.feedback: Vertical erosion dominates upstream; lateral erosion and deposition increase downstream.

misconceptions.misconception: Solution is a type of erosion only.
misconceptions.feedback: Solution is both an erosion process and a transport process.

specification_points.title: Fluvial landforms of erosion and deposition

misconceptions.misconception: Waterfalls form where soft rock is above hard rock.
misconceptions.feedback: Hard rock lies over soft rock; the soft rock is eroded faster, undercutting the hard rock.

misconceptions.misconception: The fastest flow is on the inside of a meander.
misconceptions.feedback: Fastest flow and erosion are on the outside bend; deposition is on the inside.

specification_points.title: Flood risk factors, hydrographs and flood management

misconceptions.misconception: Lag time is the time of peak discharge.
misconceptions.feedback: Lag time is the time between peak rainfall and peak discharge.

misconceptions.misconception: Urban areas reduce flood risk.
misconceptions.feedback: Impermeable surfaces increase surface runoff and shorten lag time.

specification_points.title: Ice extent and glacial processes

misconceptions.misconception: Glaciers erode by melting.
misconceptions.feedback: They erode by plucking and abrasion; freeze-thaw supplies rock fragments.

misconceptions.misconception: The whole UK was covered by ice.
misconceptions.feedback: Ice reached roughly a line from the Severn to the Thames; the south was ice-free.

specification_points.title: Glacial landforms of erosion and deposition

misconceptions.misconception: A U-shaped valley is formed by a river.
misconceptions.feedback: Glacial troughs are formed by glaciers eroding the valley floor and sides.

misconceptions.misconception: Erratics are rocks from the local area.
misconceptions.feedback: Erratics are rocks of a different type carried by ice from elsewhere.

specification_points.title: Glaciated upland areas: economic activities, conflicts and tourism management

misconceptions.misconception: Tourism only has positive effects.
misconceptions.feedback: Tourism brings income but also congestion, footpath erosion and high house prices.

misconceptions.misconception: Conservation and development never conflict.
misconceptions.feedback: Quarrying, forestry and tourism can conflict with conservation.

specification_points.title: Urbanisation: global patterns, migration, natural increase and megacities

misconceptions.misconception: Urbanisation means a city getting bigger in area.
misconceptions.feedback: Urbanisation is an increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas.

misconceptions.misconception: Most urban growth is in HICs.
misconceptions.feedback: The fastest urban growth is in LICs and NEEs.

specification_points.title: A major city in an LIC or NEE: growth, opportunities, challenges and urban planning

misconceptions.misconception: Squatter settlements have no positive features.
misconceptions.feedback: They often have strong communities and informal jobs, and can be improved by self-help schemes.

misconceptions.misconception: Everyone who moves to the city finds a formal job.
misconceptions.feedback: Many work in the informal economy without contracts or tax.

specification_points.title: UK cities: distribution, a major UK city, opportunities, challenges and regeneration

misconceptions.misconception: Brownfield sites are green areas.
misconceptions.feedback: Brownfield sites have been built on before; greenfield sites have not.

misconceptions.misconception: Regeneration means only building new houses.
misconceptions.feedback: Regeneration improves an area economically, socially and environmentally.

specification_points.title: Sustainable urban living and urban transport strategies

misconceptions.misconception: Sustainable means only using renewable energy.
misconceptions.feedback: It means meeting needs now without harming future generations: water, energy, waste, green space and transport.

misconceptions.misconception: Building more roads always reduces congestion.
misconceptions.feedback: New roads can attract more traffic; public transport and charging reduce car use.

specification_points.title: Measuring development, the Demographic Transition Model, causes and consequences of uneven development

misconceptions.misconception: GNI alone shows quality of life.
misconceptions.feedback: GNI is an average; HDI combines income, health and education.

misconceptions.misconception: Death rates are lowest in LICs.
misconceptions.feedback: Death rates fall as countries develop; birth rates fall later (DTM stages 2-3).

specification_points.title: Strategies to reduce the development gap, including tourism

misconceptions.misconception: Aid always helps development.
misconceptions.feedback: Aid can be misused or create dependency; it works best when targeted and long term.

misconceptions.misconception: Fairtrade means goods are free.
misconceptions.feedback: Fairtrade guarantees producers a fair minimum price and a premium for community projects.

specification_points.title: Rapid economic development in an LIC or NEE: TNCs, trade, aid, environment and quality of life

misconceptions.misconception: TNCs only bring benefits.
misconceptions.feedback: TNCs bring jobs and investment but profits may leave the country and conditions can be poor.

misconceptions.misconception: Economic growth always improves the environment.
misconceptions.feedback: Growth often increases pollution and resource use.

specification_points.title: Economic change in the UK: deindustrialisation, post-industrial economy, rural change, transport, north-south divide

misconceptions.misconception: Most UK workers are in manufacturing.
misconceptions.feedback: Most now work in the tertiary (services) and quaternary sectors.

misconceptions.misconception: The north-south divide is only about weather.
misconceptions.feedback: It describes differences in wealth, health, jobs and house prices.

specification_points.title: Resources: significance of food, water and energy and global inequalities

misconceptions.misconception: Resources are shared equally around the world.
misconceptions.feedback: HICs consume far more per person than LICs.

misconceptions.misconception: Resources only matter for economic growth.
misconceptions.feedback: They are essential for health and social well-being too.

specification_points.title: UK food: demand for high-value exports, seasonal produce, food miles, agribusiness

misconceptions.misconception: Food miles only measure distance.
misconceptions.feedback: They are used to show the carbon footprint of transporting food.

misconceptions.misconception: Agribusiness means small family farms.
misconceptions.feedback: Agribusiness is large-scale, intensive, commercial farming.

specification_points.title: UK water: demand, quality and pollution, deficit and surplus, water transfers

misconceptions.misconception: The UK has water surplus everywhere.
misconceptions.feedback: The south east has a deficit; the north and west have a surplus.

misconceptions.misconception: Water transfers have no disadvantages.
misconceptions.feedback: They are expensive and can harm ecosystems and anger donor areas.

specification_points.title: UK energy: changing energy mix, declining fossil fuels, issues of exploitation

misconceptions.misconception: The UK still produces most of its own coal.
misconceptions.feedback: Domestic coal production has collapsed; the UK imports fuel and uses more renewables.

misconceptions.misconception: Renewables have no disadvantages.
misconceptions.feedback: They can be intermittent, costly and visually intrusive.

specification_points.title: Food: global demand, food security and insecurity, factors and impacts

misconceptions.misconception: Food insecurity means a food deficit.
misconceptions.feedback: Food insecurity is lacking reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food.

misconceptions.misconception: Food insecurity only causes hunger.
misconceptions.feedback: It also causes undernutrition, soil erosion, rising prices and social unrest.

specification_points.title: Food: strategies to increase supply and sustainable food supplies

misconceptions.misconception: The green revolution was entirely positive.
misconceptions.feedback: It raised yields but needed costly fertilisers, pesticides and water.

misconceptions.misconception: Hydroponics needs soil.
misconceptions.feedback: Hydroponics grows plants in nutrient-rich water without soil.

specification_points.title: Water: global demand, water security and insecurity, factors and impacts

misconceptions.misconception: Water insecurity only happens in deserts.
misconceptions.feedback: Pollution, over-abstraction, poverty and poor infrastructure also cause it.

misconceptions.misconception: Water insecurity means a water deficit.
misconceptions.feedback: It means not having reliable access to enough clean, affordable water.

specification_points.title: Water: strategies to increase supply and sustainable water supplies

misconceptions.misconception: Desalination is cheap.
misconceptions.feedback: It is expensive and uses a lot of energy.

misconceptions.misconception: Grey water is dirty sewage.
misconceptions.feedback: Grey water is lightly used water from baths/sinks that can be reused, eg for toilets or gardens.

specification_points.title: Energy: global demand, energy security and insecurity, factors and impacts

misconceptions.misconception: Energy insecurity means an energy deficit.
misconceptions.feedback: It means not having reliable, affordable access to enough energy.

misconceptions.misconception: Energy supply depends only on geology.
misconceptions.feedback: Cost, technology and politics also affect supply.

specification_points.title: Energy: strategies to increase supply and sustainable energy

misconceptions.misconception: Nuclear power is renewable.
misconceptions.feedback: Nuclear is non-renewable (uranium) though low carbon.

misconceptions.misconception: Sustainable energy only means building wind farms.
misconceptions.feedback: It also means reducing demand, conservation and efficiency.

specification_points.title: Issue evaluation: interpreting resources, stakeholders and justifying decisions

misconceptions.misconception: Only one side of an issue needs considering.
misconceptions.feedback: Consider advantages and disadvantages for different stakeholders, then justify a choice.

misconceptions.misconception: A decision needs no evidence.
misconceptions.feedback: Use evidence from the resource booklet to support the decision.

specification_points.title: Fieldwork: suitable enquiry questions, theory, locations and risk

misconceptions.misconception: Any location is suitable for fieldwork.
misconceptions.feedback: Locations must be safe, accessible and allow relevant data to be collected.

misconceptions.misconception: Risk assessment is only about weather.
misconceptions.feedback: Risks include traffic, tides, slippery rocks and water; each needs a way to reduce it.

specification_points.title: Fieldwork: selecting, measuring and recording data; sampling

misconceptions.misconception: Primary data means the most important data.
misconceptions.feedback: Primary data is collected yourself; secondary data comes from other sources.

misconceptions.misconception: Random sampling means choosing places you like.
misconceptions.feedback: Random sampling gives every point an equal chance of being chosen (eg random number tables).

specification_points.title: Fieldwork: processing and presenting data

misconceptions.misconception: Any graph will do.
misconceptions.feedback: Choose a method that suits the data, eg scatter graph for relationships.

misconceptions.misconception: Pie charts show change over time.
misconceptions.feedback: Line graphs show change over time; pie charts show proportions.

specification_points.title: Fieldwork: describing, analysing and explaining data; anomalies

misconceptions.misconception: Anomalies should be ignored.
misconceptions.feedback: Anomalies should be identified and explained.

misconceptions.misconception: Describing and explaining are the same.
misconceptions.feedback: Describe what the data shows; explain why using geographical knowledge.

specification_points.title: Fieldwork: reaching conclusions

misconceptions.misconception: A conclusion just repeats the results.
misconceptions.feedback: A conclusion answers the enquiry question using evidence.

misconceptions.misconception: Conclusions are always certain.
misconceptions.feedback: Conclusions should say how far the evidence supports the hypothesis.

specification_points.title: Fieldwork: evaluating the enquiry

misconceptions.misconception: Evaluation means saying the fieldwork was good.
misconceptions.feedback: Evaluation identifies problems, limitations and improvements, and judges reliability.

misconceptions.misconception: Reliable and accurate mean the same.
misconceptions.feedback: Reliable = repeatable/consistent; accurate = close to the true value.

specification_points.title: Cartographic skills: atlas maps, latitude and longitude, patterns

misconceptions.misconception: Latitude lines run north-south.
misconceptions.feedback: Lines of latitude run east-west and measure distance north or south of the Equator.

misconceptions.misconception: A pattern is described by listing places.
misconceptions.feedback: Describe the overall pattern: where most/least, clusters, along coasts, exceptions.

specification_points.title: Cartographic skills: OS maps, grid references, scale, direction, relief

misconceptions.misconception: Grid references go up then along.
misconceptions.feedback: Along the corridor (eastings) then up the stairs (northings).

misconceptions.misconception: Contour lines close together mean flat land.
misconceptions.feedback: Close contours mean steep land; widely spaced contours mean gentle slopes.

specification_points.title: Graphical skills: choosing, completing and interpreting graphs and maps

misconceptions.misconception: A choropleth map uses symbols.
misconceptions.feedback: A choropleth uses shading by category; proportional symbols use sized symbols.

misconceptions.misconception: Scatter graphs show change over time.
misconceptions.feedback: Scatter graphs show the relationship between two variables.

specification_points.title: Numerical skills: number, area, scale, proportion, ratio and magnitude

misconceptions.misconception: A scale of 1:50 000 means 1 cm = 50 km.
misconceptions.feedback: 1 cm on the map = 50 000 cm = 500 m on the ground.

misconceptions.misconception: Proportion and number are the same.
misconceptions.feedback: A proportion is a part of a whole, often a fraction or percentage.

specification_points.title: Statistical skills: averages, range, quartiles, percentage change, trends

misconceptions.misconception: The median is the average of all values.
misconceptions.feedback: The median is the middle value when the data is in order.

misconceptions.misconception: Percentage change = new - old.
misconceptions.feedback: Percentage change = (new - old) ÷ old × 100.

questions.answer: Some places have a high population density, so more people could be killed. Poverty means people cannot afford strong buildings, so damage is greater. Places near plate margins or coasts are more exposed.

questions.question: Using named examples, compare the effects of tectonic hazards in two areas of contrasting levels of wealth.
questions.answer: In Chile (an HIC/NEE) in 2010 the magnitude 8.8 earthquake killed about 500 people because building codes meant fewer buildings collapsed, but the economic cost was about $30 billion. In Nepal (an LIC) in 2015 about 9,000 people died and 3 million were made homeless because houses were poorly built, and aid was slow to reach remote villages.

self_check.model_answer: In Chile (an HIC/NEE) in 2010 the magnitude 8.8 earthquake killed about 500 people because building codes meant fewer buildings collapsed, but the economic cost was about $30 billion. In Nepal (an LIC) in 2015 about 9,000 people died and 3 million were made homeless because houses were poorly built, and aid was slow to reach remote villages.

questions.question: Explain why the immediate responses to an earthquake may be slower in an LIC than in an HIC.
questions.answer: LICs have less money for trained rescue teams and equipment, so rescue is slower. Roads are often poor or blocked by landslides, so remote villages cannot be reached for days. They rely on international aid, which takes time to arrive.
questions.mark_scheme: Levels of response: Level 1 (Basic) 1-2; Level 2 (Clear) 3-4. Indicative content: lack of money / equipment / emergency services; damaged or poor roads / remote areas; relies on international aid which takes time to arrive; communications damaged / poor organisation / corruption.
questions.model_answer: LICs have less money for trained rescue teams and equipment, so rescue is slower. Roads are often poor or blocked by landslides, so remote villages cannot be reached for days. They rely on international aid, which takes time to arrive.
common_misconceptions: Secondary effects happen at the same time as the earthquake.
Richer countries always have more deaths because more is built.

questions.answer: Seismometers detect small earthquakes as magma rises, and tiltmeters show the ground swelling. These signs mean an eruption can be predicted so people can be evacuated in time.

questions.question: To what extent can monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce the effects of tectonic hazards?
questions.answer: Monitoring volcanoes with seismometers and tiltmeters means eruptions can be predicted so people can evacuate, which saves lives. Earthquake-proof buildings with cross-bracing are less likely to collapse, so fewer people die, as in Japan. However, earthquakes cannot be predicted accurately and these strategies are expensive, so LICs such as Nepal cannot afford them. Overall, I think they reduce effects to a large extent in HICs because they can afford them, but only to a limited extent in LICs.

questions.question: Explain how tropical storms form.
questions.answer: Warm ocean water (at least 27°C) evaporates and the warm, moist air rises, creating low pressure. As it rises it cools and condenses, forming cumulonimbus clouds and releasing heat, which gives the storm more energy. More air is drawn in, and the Coriolis effect makes the storm spin.
questions.mark_scheme: Levels of response: Level 1 (Basic) 1-2; Level 2 (Clear) 3-4. Indicative content: warm ocean water evaporates / warm moist air rises; air cools and condenses, forming cumulonimbus clouds and releasing heat; more air drawn in creating strong winds; the Coriolis effect makes the storm spin; eye forms where air sinks; moves with prevailing winds and weakens over land.

questions.question: Using a named example of a tropical storm, assess the extent to which its effects were reduced by the responses.
questions.answer: Typhoon Haiyan hit the Philippines in 2013. Over 6,000 people died, mainly because a 5 m storm surge flooded Tacloban, and about 4 million people were made homeless. Shortages of clean water caused disease. Around 800,000 people were evacuated, which reduced deaths, and international aid such as food, water and field hospitals arrived, which stopped disease spreading. Long-term, cyclone shelters were built and mangroves replanted so future storms will cause fewer deaths. However, aid was slow to reach remote islands because roads were blocked. Overall, I think the responses reduced the effects to some extent because evacuation saved many lives, but the storm surge was not expected so many still died.

Indicative content: primary effects: deaths, destruction, flooding; secondary effects: disease, homelessness, food and water shortages; economic effects: jobs, crops, businesses; immediate responses: evacuation, rescue, emergency aid; long-term responses: rebuilding, shelters, mangroves, warnings; limits: slow aid, poor access, corruption.

self_check.model_answer: Typhoon Haiyan hit the Philippines in 2013. Over 6,000 people died, mainly because a 5 m storm surge flooded Tacloban, and about 4 million people were made homeless. Shortages of clean water caused disease. Around 800,000 people were evacuated, which reduced deaths, and international aid such as food, water and field hospitals arrived, which stopped disease spreading. Long-term, cyclone shelters were built and mangroves replanted so future storms will cause fewer deaths. However, aid was slow to reach remote islands because roads were blocked. Overall, I think the responses reduced the effects to some extent because evacuation saved many lives, but the storm surge was not expected so many still died.

questions.question: Using a named example, explain the social, economic and environmental impacts of an extreme weather event in the UK.
questions.answer: In the Somerset Levels floods of 2014, about 600 homes were flooded and villages such as Muchelney were cut off for weeks, so people relied on boats. Around 14,000 hectares of farmland were flooded, which cost farmers millions as cattle had to be moved. Sewage contaminated floodwater, which damaged habitats.

questions.mark_scheme: 1 mark per different valid point (max 2). Valid points include: changing farming (drought-resistant crops / irrigation); managing water supply (reservoirs, desalination, meters); reducing risk from rising sea levels (sea walls, raising buildings); heat measures (shade, cooling, green roofs).
questions.model_answer: Building sea walls and growing drought-resistant crops.
common_misconceptions: Mitigation and adaptation mean the same thing.
Planting trees is adaptation.

questions.question: 'Mitigation is more important than adaptation in managing climate change.' Do you agree?
questions.answer: Mitigation, such as renewable energy and the Paris Agreement, tackles the causes by cutting emissions, so warming slows for everyone in the long term. However, adaptation, such as sea walls and drought-resistant crops, protects people now from changes already happening, which is vital for poorer countries that emit little but suffer most. Overall, I agree to a large extent because without mitigation adaptation will become impossible, but both are needed.

questions.question: Explain how nutrients are cycled in an ecosystem.
questions.answer: Plants take up nutrients from the soil. Animals eat the plants so nutrients pass along the food chain. When they die, leaf litter and dead animals are broken down by decomposers, returning the nutrients to the soil.
questions.mark_scheme: 1+1+1 or point + developed point(s) (d), max 3. Two basic points can gain 2 marks. questions.model_answer: Plants take up nutrients from the soil. Animals eat the plants so nutrients pass along the food chain. When they die, leaf litter and dead animals are broken down by decomposers, returning the nutrients to the soil.

Changing one component only affects that species.

questions.question: Explain why rainforest soils are nutrient-poor even though the forest is very lush.
questions.answer: Heavy rain leaches nutrients out of the soil. Dead leaves decompose quickly in the hot, wet climate and the nutrients are taken up quickly by plants, so most nutrients are stored in the biomass rather than the soil.

questions.question: Using a case study of a tropical rainforest, evaluate whether the economic benefits of deforestation outweigh the environmental costs.
questions.answer: In the Amazon, Brazil earns billions from exporting soya and beef, and cattle ranching provides jobs, so incomes rise. Roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway and HEP from Belo Monte help development. However, about 17% of the forest has been lost, which destroys habitats and reduces biodiversity, and burning releases CO2, adding to climate change. Soil erosion makes land infertile after a few years so benefits are short-term. Overall, I do not think the benefits outweigh the costs because the environmental damage is long-term and global, while the profits mostly go to large companies.

questions.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of strategies used to manage tropical rainforests sustainably.
questions.answer: Selective logging allows the forest to regrow, so timber is available for future generations, and ecotourism gives local people an income from protecting the forest. However, illegal logging continues because laws are hard to enforce in remote areas, and demand for beef and soya makes clearing more profitable. Overall, I think the strategies are effective to some extent because they protect particular areas, but they are too small-scale to stop large-scale clearance.

questions.question: Using a case study, assess the opportunities and challenges of developing a hot desert environment.
questions.answer: In the Thar Desert, the Indira Gandhi Canal allows irrigated farming, and mining of gypsum and limestone creates jobs. Wind and solar farms generate renewable energy, and tourists visit Jaisalmer for camel safaris, which brings income. However, temperatures reach 50°C, water supply is limited and irrigation causes salinisation, and the area is remote with poor roads, which makes development expensive. Overall, I think the opportunities outweigh the challenges because technology such as the canal has overcome the water problem to a large extent.

questions.question: Using a case study, discuss the opportunities and challenges of economic development in a cold environment.
questions.answer: In Alaska, oil at Prudhoe Bay provides thousands of jobs, which brings income and taxes, and fishing for salmon and tourism bring income. However, temperatures fall below -40°C, so working outside is dangerous, and the area is remote, so supplies are expensive. Buildings and the 1,300 km Trans-Alaska pipeline must be raised on piles so they do not melt the permafrost, which makes development expensive.

questions.question: To what extent is it possible to balance the needs of economic development and conservation in cold environments?
questions.answer: Technology such as the raised Trans-Alaska pipeline lets caribou migrate and prevents melting of permafrost, and the Antarctic Treaty bans mining, so conservation can be balanced with development. However, demand for oil creates pressure to drill in protected areas, and spills such as the Exxon Valdez in 1989 still happen. Overall, I think a balance is possible to some extent because technology and laws reduce damage, but accidents and climate change mean the environment is still harmed.

questions.question: Explain how freeze-thaw weathering breaks down rock on cliffs.
questions.answer: Water enters cracks in the rock and freezes at night. Ice expands by about 9%, putting pressure on the rock. When it thaws and refreezes many times, the crack widens until pieces break off.

questions.question: Explain how longshore drift transports material along a coast.

questions.question: Explain how headlands and bays are formed.
questions.answer: The coastline has alternating bands of hard and soft rock. The soft rock (eg clay) is eroded faster by hydraulic power and abrasion, forming bays. The hard rock (eg chalk) is more resistant so it is eroded more slowly and is left sticking out as a headland. Bays are then sheltered so beaches form.

questions.question: Explain how a wave-cut platform is formed.

questions.question: Explain the formation of a stack.
questions.answer: Waves erode a crack in the headland by hydraulic power and abrasion, which widens it into a cave. The cave is eroded through the headland to form an arch. Weathering and erosion weaken the roof of the arch until it collapses, leaving a stack separated from the headland, which may later be eroded into a stump.

questions.question: Explain how a spit is formed.
questions.answer: Longshore drift moves sand and shingle along the coast. Where the coastline changes direction at an estuary, the material is deposited out into the sea because the waves lose energy, which builds a long ridge. Changes in wind direction curve the end, and a salt marsh forms in the sheltered water behind.

questions.question: Using an example of a coastal management scheme in the UK, explain the reasons for management and the conflicts it caused.
questions.answer: At Mappleton on the Holderness coast, the soft boulder clay cliffs erode by about 2 m a year, threatening homes and the B1242 road, so in 1991 rock armour and two rock groynes were built for £2 million. The groynes trapped sediment, but this starved beaches further south, so erosion increased at Cowden, which caused conflict because residents there were not protected.

questions.question: Explain how a waterfall and gorge are formed.
questions.answer: A band of hard rock lies on top of soft rock. The soft rock is eroded faster by hydraulic action and abrasion, which undercuts the hard rock and forms a plunge pool. The overhang becomes unstable so it collapses, and the waterfall retreats upstream, which leaves a steep-sided gorge.

questions.question: Explain how an ox-bow lake is formed.
questions.answer: On the outside of a meander the fastest flow erodes the bank by hydraulic action and abrasion, which forms a river cliff, while slower flow on the inside deposits sediment because the water loses energy. Erosion on the outside bends makes the neck narrow. During a flood the river cuts through the neck because it takes the shortest route, and deposition seals off the old meander, which leaves an ox-bow lake.

questions.question: Explain how urbanisation increases the risk of flooding.
questions.answer: Concrete and tarmac are impermeable, so water cannot infiltrate and runs off over the surface. Drains carry it quickly to the river, so lag time is shorter and peak discharge is higher.

questions.question: Using an example of a flood management scheme in the UK, assess the social, economic and environmental issues it raised.
questions.answer: In Banbury, a flood storage area was built for £18.5 million after floods in 1998 and 2007. Socially, it protects over 400 homes so residents feel safer, and economically it protects businesses and the M40, saving about £100 million of damage. Environmentally, the storage area created new wetland habitats, but building the embankment disturbed farmland. Overall, I think the scheme was successful because the economic benefits are much greater than the cost.

questions.question: Explain how freeze-thaw weathering supplies material to glaciers.
questions.answer: Water in cracks freezes and expands by 9%, widening the cracks. After repeated freezing and thawing, rock breaks off and falls onto the glacier, which carries it away and uses it for abrasion.

questions.question: Explain how a corrie is formed.
questions.answer: Snow collects in a north-facing hollow and compacts into ice. The ice moves by rotational slip; plucking steepens the back wall and abrasion deepens the floor, which makes the hollow deeper. Less erosion at the front leaves a rock lip, so when the ice melts a tarn may fill the hollow.
questions.mark_scheme: Levels of response: Level 1 (Basic) 1-2; Level 2 (Clear) 3-4. Indicative content: snow collects in a hollow (often north-facing) and compacts into ice; rotational slip; plucking steepens the back wall; abrasion deepens the hollow; rock lip forms at the front; tarn when ice melts; freeze-thaw weathering on the back wall.
questions.model_answer: Snow collects in a north-facing hollow and compacts into ice. The ice moves by rotational slip; plucking steepens the back wall and abrasion deepens the floor, which makes the hollow deeper. Less erosion at the front leaves a rock lip, so when the ice melts a tarn may fill the hollow.
common_misconceptions: A U-shaped valley is formed by a river.
Erratics are rocks from the local area.

questions.question: Explain how a glacial trough (U-shaped valley) is formed.
questions.answer: A glacier follows an existing V-shaped river valley and erodes its sides and floor by abrasion and plucking, so it is deepened and widened into a U shape with steep sides and a flat floor. Interlocking spurs are cut off because the ice cannot flow round them, which leaves truncated spurs.

questions.question: Using an example of a glaciated upland area used for tourism, evaluate the strategies used to manage the impact of tourism.
questions.answer: In the Lake District, which has about 18 million visitors a year, Fix the Fells repairs footpaths with stone pitching, which reduces erosion. A 10 mph speed limit on Windermere reduces noise and pollution. However, repairs are expensive and rely on volunteers, and congestion in towns like Ambleside remains because most people still arrive by car. Overall, I think the strategies are effective to some extent because they reduce erosion, but visitor numbers are too high to solve traffic problems.

questions.question: Using a case study of a major city in an LIC or NEE, discuss the challenges created by urban growth.
questions.answer: In Rio de Janeiro about 1.5 million people live in favelas such as Rocinha, where houses are poorly built on steep slopes and at risk from landslides. Many lack sanitation, so sewage pollutes Guanabara Bay, which spreads disease. Unemployment is high and drug gangs control some favelas, so crime rates are high. Traffic congestion causes air pollution.

questions.question: Using a named UK city, evaluate whether urban change has created more economic or more social opportunities.
questions.answer: In London, the regeneration of the Lower Lea Valley for the 2012 Olympics created thousands of jobs and attracted Westfield Stratford, which brought economic benefits. Canary Wharf provides over 100,000 jobs in finance. Socially, London's cultural mix brings festivals such as the Notting Hill Carnival, and the Olympic Park created new green spaces and sports facilities for local people. However, many new homes are too expensive for locals. Overall, I think urban change has created more economic opportunities, because the jobs benefit the whole city while social benefits are unequal.
questions.mark_scheme: Levels of response: Level 1 (Basic) 1-3; Level 2 (Clear) 4-6; Level 3 (Detailed) 7-9. Indicative content: economic: new jobs / business / regeneration; economic: integrated transport / infrastructure; economic: tourism / retail; social: cultural mix / festivals / food; social: recreation / entertainment / green spaces; social: housing, education and health improvements.

questions.question: Using an example of an LIC or NEE, evaluate how far tourism has helped to reduce the development gap.
questions.answer: In Jamaica, tourism employs over 200,000 people and earns about a fifth of GDP, so people have regular incomes and taxes pay for roads and services. However, many all-inclusive hotels are foreign-owned so profits leak abroad, and jobs are often seasonal and low paid. Overall, I think tourism has reduced the development gap to some extent, because it brings jobs and income, but leakage limits the benefits for local people.

questions.question: Using a case study of an LIC or NEE, evaluate whether economic development has improved quality of life more than it has harmed the environment.
questions.answer: In Nigeria, economic growth from oil and TNCs such as Shell has created jobs, and incomes have risen, so more people can afford healthcare and education; life expectancy has increased. However, oil spills in the Niger Delta have polluted water and farmland, which damages fishing and farming livelihoods, and Lagos suffers air pollution and congestion. Overall, I think development has improved quality of life for many people, but the environmental costs fall hardest on the poorest communities, so the benefits are not shared equally.

self_check.model_answer: In Nigeria, economic growth from oil and TNCs such as Shell has created jobs, and incomes have risen, so more people can afford healthcare and education; life expectancy has increased. However, oil spills in the Niger Delta have polluted water and farmland, which damages fishing and farming livelihoods, and Lagos suffers air pollution and congestion. Overall, I think development has improved quality of life for many people, but the environmental costs fall hardest on the poorest communities, so the benefits are not shared equally.

questions.question: Using an example of a large-scale agricultural development, assess its advantages and disadvantages.
questions.answer: In Almería, Spain, about 30,000 hectares of greenhouses produce vegetables all year for export to Europe, which creates thousands of jobs and earns billions of euros. However, irrigation is depleting the aquifers, so water supplies may run out, and plastic waste pollutes the land and sea, which harms wildlife. Overall, I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages economically, because the region has become wealthy, but the scheme is not sustainable unless water use is reduced.

questions.question: Using an example of a large-scale water transfer scheme, assess its advantages and disadvantages.
questions.answer: China's South-North Water Transfer Project moves water from the Yangtze to Beijing, which supplies millions of people and industry in the dry north. However, it cost over $60 billion, about 330,000 people were relocated, so communities were broken up, and pollution along the route affects water quality. Overall, I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages because Beijing's water shortage threatened the economy, but the social and environmental costs are high.

questions.question: Using an example of fossil fuel extraction, assess its advantages and disadvantages.
questions.answer: Fracking at Preston New Road in Lancashire could provide gas for decades, which would reduce the UK's reliance on imports and create jobs. However, it caused earthquakes of up to magnitude 2.9 in 2019, which worried residents, it risks contaminating groundwater, and burning gas releases CO2, which adds to climate change. Overall, I think the disadvantages outweigh the advantages because of climate change and strong local opposition, which is why fracking was paused.

questions.question: A new cruise ship terminal and port are proposed for a small island. Using the resources and your own understanding, should the development go ahead? Justify your decision.
questions.answer: The terminal would bring more cruise passengers, who spend money in local shops, creating jobs and tax income for services. The current port facilities are inadequate, so regeneration would also help trade. However, dredging would damage coral reefs, which attract long-stay divers, and cruise ships cause pollution. Cruise passengers stay only a few hours, so they spend less than long-stay tourists. Overall, I think the development should go ahead only at a smaller scale, because the port improvements are needed but the reefs are vital for the long-term tourist economy.

questions.question: Assess the effectiveness of the data presentation techniques you used in your physical geography enquiry.
questions.answer: A scatter graph of width against distance downstream with a line of best fit was effective because it clearly showed a positive correlation and made anomalies easy to spot. Cross-sections drawn to scale were effective because they showed how the channel became wider and deeper, which helped us test the Bradshaw model. However, the scatter graph could not show why width changed, and the cross-sections were cluttered with only three sites. Overall, I think the techniques were mostly effective because they showed the relationships needed to test our hypothesis.

Indicative content: scatter graph with line of best fit shows the relationship / correlation; cross-sections drawn to scale show channel shape; annotated photos / sketches show features; proportional symbols on a map show spatial pattern; limitations: hard to compare / cannot show cause / only at sites; improvements: different scale, more data points.

questions.question: For one of your fieldwork enquiries, to what extent did your data help you obtain accurate results and reach a valid conclusion?
questions.answer: Our river enquiry used five sites, which is a small sample, so the results may not represent the whole river. The float method for velocity was affected by wind, so it was not very accurate. However, we took three readings at each site and calculated a mean, which reduced the effect of errors, and Environment Agency data supported our findings. Overall, I think the data helped us reach a valid conclusion to some extent, because the trend matched the Bradshaw model, but more sites and better equipment would have made it more reliable.
